summary:
Using real satellite fire data, we built a forecast model, a live dashboard, and a FireGuard strategy game that drops you into real fire hotspots and asks you to make the calls a firefighter makes.
A dashboard tells you what is happening. A strategy game makes you decide what to do about it.
The dashboard is for the people scientists, activists, and firefighters who fight fires for a living. They look at the burning calendar, see that this month is above normal, and plan.
The game is for everyone else. It gives you a fire station, ten countries, a few crews, and the same calendar. When a month is above normal, the fire you play is harder. You feel why the number matters because you run out of crews if you ignore it.
So the two are the same data told two ways: the dashboard for people who need to read it and the game for people who need to understand it and spread awareness.
details:
The website shows emergency managers when a region burns more than usual; the game makes anyone feel it, using the same harmonized data.

The challenge asked for a tool that turns two decades of MODIS and VIIRS hotspots into a burning calendar people can act on. The web app does that for professionals. But a calendar only informs people who already care. The game takes the same harmonized record and turns it into decisions: you run a fire station, you see each country’s calendar strip and whether this month is above its twenty-year median, and that anomaly changes the mission you play. Students, judges, and the public understand “this November in the UAE is 1.7 times its usual burning” far faster when it means an extra flare-up they have to fight. The game is the outreach layer of the same product, not a separate idea.

Same data, two audiences. Managers need numbers; everyone else needs a reason to look at them.

The game teaches the concepts the challenge is about: seasonality, anomalies against a median, limited crews, and the cost of a wrong allocation.

It is honest about science. Risk indices are labelled as relative, not probabilities; nothing in the game invents a fire; a month with no data says so.

Yesterday the connection was invisible; today the game reads the site’s own calendar and the anomaly changes the mission, so the two halves tell one story.
